name: LangGraph Thread / Checkpointer Model
description: LangGraph's persistence architecture: thread_id-keyed checkpoints written after every graph step (short-term, thread-scoped state), with pluggable backends — Redis (TTL, fast, in-memory) and MongoDB (document, durable) for checkpointers, and PostgresSaver as the standard production path. A separate cross-thread Store (BaseStore: RedisStore / MongoDBStore / PostgresStore) provides namespaced key-value long-term memory at the user/application level. The directly applicable reference architecture for Labmate given its existing MongoDB + Redis + LangGraph stack.

identity_and_auth.user_identity_model: LangGraph itself is identity-agnostic infrastructure — it does not authenticate users. Identity is expressed as values the application supplies in the runtime config: thread_id scopes a conversation, and a user_id is conventionally passed (in configurable, and as the leading element of a Store namespace, e.g. (user_id, 'memories')) to scope cross-thread long-term memory to an individual. There is no built-in OAuth/SSO/API-key login at the persistence layer; the embedding application (e.g. Labmate's Discord connector) is responsible for authenticating the user and mapping that to user_id/thread_id. Multi-tenancy is achieved by partitioning on thread_id (per task/conversation) and namespacing the Store by user/org.
identity_and_auth.multi_user_collaboration: No native team/role/permission model in the persistence layer; isolation is logical, via keys. Different users and tasks are kept separate by distinct thread_ids (checkpoints) and distinct Store namespaces (long-term memory). Shared/cross-thread knowledge is modeled by choosing a shared namespace (e.g. an org- or app-level namespace in the Store) rather than a per-user one. Concurrent access to the same thread is possible but the model is optimistic/last-write-style at the checkpoint level; collaboration features (sharing, roles) must be built by the application on top of these keys. [uncertain]

workspace_model.workspace_definition: A 'workspace' is virtual and key-based, not a directory or repo. The primary scoping unit is the thread (thread_id) representing one conversation/task/run; a coarser 'workspace' (project/user/org) is an application-level convention layered via the Store namespace and/or fields in configurable. LangGraph provides the thread + namespace primitives; the application decides what a workspace means (e.g. Labmate workspace_id) and maps it onto thread_id grouping and Store namespaces. There is no filesystem/git binding — everything is an entry in the configured backend (Redis/Mongo/Postgres).
workspace_model.workspace_session_binding: Sessions == threads, identified by thread_id and supplied per call in config={'configurable': {'thread_id': ...}}. State is reconstructed from the latest checkpoint for that thread on resume. A user can have many threads (sessions), and many threads can belong to one logical workspace by application convention. Multiple concurrent threads run independently (multi-tenant by design). Within a thread, checkpoints are ordered and addressable, so resumption picks up from the last (or any specified) checkpoint. checkpoint_ns subdivides state within a thread (e.g. for subgraphs/namespaced channels).
workspace_model.context_scoping: Two architectural tiers. Thread-scoped (short-term / 'working memory'): the graph State for a thread — conversation history and node channel values — persisted as checkpoints by the checkpointer; lost-to-other-threads by design. Cross-thread (long-term): application-defined data in the Store (BaseStore), addressed by namespace + key, shared across threads (e.g. user preferences, learned facts, shared knowledge). Optional semantic layer (LangMem / vector-enabled stores) adds episodic/procedural memory on top of the Store. Configuration/tool wiring is supplied by the application at compile/invoke time, not persisted as workspace config by LangGraph itself.
workspace_model.config_file_instruction_precedence: Not a file/instruction-cascade product — there are no AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md/.rules files. 'Configuration' is the runtime config dict (configurable: thread_id, checkpoint_ns, checkpoint_id, user_id, etc.) plus the graph definition (nodes, state schema, compiled checkpointer/store). Behavioral instructions (system prompts, policies) are part of application code/state, and 'precedence' is whatever ordering the application encodes when assembling prompts/state. Any CLAUDE.md-style layered instruction precedence is the application's responsibility, not LangGraph's. [uncertain]
workspace_model.source_corpus_grounding_scope: No built-in bounded-source-corpus / notebook concept. Retrieval grounding is application-built: long-term facts/documents are stored in the Store (key-value JSON, optionally with vector embeddings for semantic search via Atlas Vector Search / RedisVL), and the application performs retrieval and injects results into thread state. There is no native notion of 'add a PDF/web/video source to scope retrieval' — the corpus is whatever the application writes to the Store or an external vector index. [uncertain]

persistence_and_history.persistence_mechanism: Hybrid, pluggable, two-system design. (1) Checkpointer (short-term): writes a checkpoint of the full graph state after every step, keyed by (thread_id, checkpoint_ns, checkpoint_id) with parent_checkpoint_id linking checkpoints chronologically. Backends: RedisSaver/AsyncRedisSaver (fast in-memory, JSON storage, TTL support), MongoDB saver (document, durable, TTL indexes), PostgresSaver (standard production reference, normalized tables checkpoints/checkpoint_blobs/checkpoint_writes). (2) Store (long-term): BaseStore implementations (RedisStore, MongoDBStore, PostgresStore) holding namespaced key-value JSON outside graph state. Storage is effectively snapshot-per-step (each checkpoint is a state snapshot) while the chain of checkpoints forms an append-style history enabling replay/time-travel; the Store is mutable key-value. Choice of backend is a code-level swap.
persistence_and_history.session_history: Per-thread checkpoint history. Each checkpoint is a StateSnapshot capturing the thread's state at one step; checkpoints are linked via parent_checkpoint_id into chronological order and are retrievable (e.g. get_state for latest, get_state_history to enumerate the sequence). This yields built-in 'time travel': you can inspect any past checkpoint by (thread_id, checkpoint_id), fork from it, or resume mid-history. Format is backend-specific JSON documents/rows (Redis JSON, Mongo documents mapping namespace+key, Postgres normalized blobs). Retention is browsable/queryable programmatically rather than via a polished end-user UI (UI is provided by LangGraph Platform / LangSmith / app layer). Portability depends on backend; state is serialized JSON so it is exportable.
persistence_and_history.memory_layering: Canonical, explicit short-term vs long-term split — the defining feature. Short-term = thread-scoped checkpointer state (current conversation, prior exchanges within the session, HITL pause/resume, fault tolerance). Long-term = cross-thread Store (BaseStore): user preferences, facts, shared knowledge that persist beyond a single conversation, addressed by namespace+key. Recommended pattern: checkpointers for within-session continuity + BaseStore for cross-session knowledge; add the LangMem SDK for semantic/procedural memory. This maps directly onto the 'ephemeral thread state vs durable cross-thread store' distinction and onto user-authored vs agent-derived memory at the application level.
persistence_and_history.search_retrieval_history: Checkpoint history is enumerable/queryable per thread (get_state_history) but is not full-text/semantic-searchable out of the box across threads. Cross-thread retrieval is the Store's job: key/namespace lookup, plus semantic search when the Store is backed by vectors (MongoDB Atlas Vector Search or RedisVL with embeddings), enabling meaning-based recall of past facts/episodes across sessions. So 'search past sessions' is achieved by writing distilled memories to the Store (optionally embedded) rather than searching raw checkpoints. Without a vector layer, retrieval is exact-key/namespace based. [uncertain]
persistence_and_history.lifecycle_ttl_cleanup: Explicit ephemeral-vs-persistent control. By default, checkpoints are persistent (no expiration) when no TTL is configured. Redis backends support TTL (ttl_config with default_ttl in minutes and refresh_on_read), and a checkpoint's TTL can be removed to 'pin' an important thread so it never expires. MongoDB supports native TTL indexes integrated with LangGraph's TTL system to auto-expire stale data. Postgres has no automatic TTL by default — production guidance is a nightly/cron DELETE job over checkpoints/checkpoint_blobs/checkpoint_writes for threads older than N days (often driven by a master conversations table with created_at/updated_at), or partitioning, since every node write creates a new checkpoint row and the table grows unbounded. This is the layer Labmate's Redis-TTL-hot + Mongo-durable-cold design maps onto directly.

execution_and_isolation.sandbox_isolation_model: LangGraph is an in-process orchestration/persistence library, not a VM/container sandbox. The graph executes inside the host application process; isolation between conversations/tenants is logical, via thread_id (state isolation) and Store namespaces (memory isolation), not OS-level sandboxing. Any container/VM isolation, network policy, or resource limits come from how the application is deployed (e.g. LangGraph Platform, your own service, serverless workers), not from the checkpointer model itself. The persistence layer guarantees state separation by key, which is the relevant 'isolation' for storage purposes. [uncertain]
execution_and_isolation.snapshot_state_restore: Strong, but for graph state rather than machine/filesystem state. The checkpointer's core feature is snapshot-and-restore of the agent's logical state: each checkpoint is a serialized snapshot of channel/state values for the thread, restorable by (thread_id[, checkpoint_id]). This enables resume-after-crash, HITL pause/resume, and time-travel/branching. It does NOT snapshot installed packages, env vars, or a filesystem image — environment reproducibility is the application/deployment's concern. State-schema migration is a known operational care-point: adding fields to the state schema can break in-flight threads on deserialize, so new fields should be optional/defaulted or the state versioned and migrated on load.
execution_and_isolation.cloud_local_handoff: Backend-portable rather than explicitly cloud<->local. Because state lives entirely in the configured backend (Redis/Mongo/Postgres) keyed by thread_id, any process with access to that backend — local, cloud, serverless worker — can resume a thread; there is no machine-pinned file. Self-hosting is fully supported (you run your own Redis/Mongo/Postgres and the open-source libraries). The common production pattern returns thread_id immediately and runs the graph asynchronously on background workers, all sharing one durable backend. [uncertain]
execution_and_isolation.parallelism_subagent_fanout: Multi-thread parallelism is first-class: distinct thread_ids run concurrently and independently, isolated by key — ideal for multi-tenant chat and parallel tasks. Within a graph, subgraphs/multi-agent structures use checkpoint_ns to namespace state per sub-component, and the same checkpointer/store can serve coordinated multi-agent systems (shared short-term memory for coordination, shared Store namespace for shared knowledge). Branching/fan-out is supported through time-travel forking: fork from a checkpoint_id to create a divergent continuation while the original thread's history is preserved. Explicit limits are deployment-defined (connection-pool sizing, recursion_limit per invoke), not fixed by the model.
execution_and_isolation.trigger_surface: Library/SDK-triggered: sessions are initiated by the application calling graph.invoke/stream with a config carrying thread_id. The embedding application defines the actual entry surface — web/API, chat connector (e.g. Discord), background jobs, HITL resume calls, or LangGraph Platform endpoints. There is no built-in CLI/IDE/Slack trigger; LangGraph supplies the runtime and persistence, and the host app supplies the trigger and auth.

implementation.implementation_stack: Open-source Python/JS framework. Core packages: langgraph-checkpoint (base interfaces, StateSnapshot, get_state/get_state_history), with backend implementations langgraph-checkpoint-redis (RedisSaver/AsyncRedisSaver + RedisStore/AsyncRedisStore; requires RedisJSON+RediSearch, bundled in Redis 8.0+ or via Redis Stack), langgraph-checkpoint-postgres (PostgresSaver; tables checkpoints/checkpoint_blobs/checkpoint_writes; one-time .setup() to create schema, run as a migration in prod), and MongoDB integrations (checkpointer + langgraph-store-mongodb MongoDBStore for cross-thread memory, long-term memories stored as JSON documents mapped to namespaces+keys, with native TTL indexes and Atlas Vector Search for semantic recall). Config keys: configurable.{thread_id, checkpoint_ns, checkpoint_id, ...}; checkpoint writes keyed by thread_id+checkpoint_ns+checkpoint_id (plus task_id, idx, channel, type, blob). Optional LangMem SDK adds semantic/procedural memory. Production guidance: PostgresSaver as standard durable path, connection pooling / PgBouncer (workers x pool.max_size < max_connections x 0.7), async runs returning thread_id immediately, recursion_limit + error handling, and scheduled checkpoint cleanup; Redis is a viable alternative if already operated.
implementation.applicability_to_labmate: Directly applicable — this is essentially Labmate's target reference architecture, because Labmate already runs MongoDB + Redis + LangGraph. Concrete mapping: use thread_id as Labmate's sessionId (one thread per Discord conversation/task); pass user_id (and a workspace_id) in configurable. Two-tier persistence: (1) Short-term checkpointer on Redis (RedisSaver) for the hot, active session state with a TTL (default_ttl + refresh_on_read), giving the fast, expiring 'active session' tier — equivalent in role to Labmate's Redis Streams active-session layer, and pin (remove TTL) for sessions that must survive; (2) long-term durable persistence on MongoDB — either the Mongo checkpointer for full thread history (cold tier) and/or, more importantly, the MongoDBStore as the cross-thread long-term memory store, namespaced by (user_id[, workspace_id], 'memories'), storing user-level facts/preferences as JSON docs with TTL indexes and Atlas Vector Search for semantic recall. This yields the exact layering Labmate wants: Redis = ephemeral thread state with TTL, Mongo = durable cross-thread memory + long-term docs, LangGraph = the orchestration tying them via thread_id. Recommendations: (a) scope all cross-thread memory by user_id (Discord identity) and group threads under workspace_id at the app layer; (b) expose history retrieval via get_state/get_state_history for resume, and build a Mongo/vector search endpoint for cross-session recall (LangGraph won't full-text-search checkpoints itself); (c) implement explicit retention (Redis TTL hot, scheduled Mongo cleanup or TTL indexes cold) — do not rely on unbounded checkpoint growth; (d) plan state-schema versioning (NotRequired/defaulted fields) to avoid breaking in-flight threads on deploy; (e) optionally add LangMem for semantic/procedural memory if the agent needs to learn across sessions. Pairs naturally with the Claude Code event-document pattern: Claude Code informs the raw append-only event log shape in Mongo, while LangGraph supplies the checkpoint/thread/Store mechanics already native to Labmate's stack.
